Hi everyone. I'm Dhruv from the Indian Institute of Science.

I have been building a Lean 4 kernel for formal Learning theory. I recently got around to formalizing all 5 conjuncts of the fundamental theorem of statistical learning plus characterization and paradigm-separation results between PAC, Online, and Gold learning.

Repo: https://github.com/Zetetic-Dhruv/formal-learning-theory-kernel
Documentation (doc-gen API, PDF (forgive the sketchy diagrams)) - https://zetetic-dhruv.github.io/formal-learning-theory-kernel/

This project has 354 theorems and no sorries so far (although I did get stuck on some stuff towards the end like universal trichotomy, made them TODOs)

The formalization exercise produced seemingly new and interesting proof techniques (like, I used approximate minimax (MWU) instead of exact minimax theorem in a constructive iterative proof replacing Moran-Yehudayoff's existential argument for compression).

I have noted any such novelty in the repo's README at the top and would love to chat if it overlaps with anyone else's interests. This is all very recent work and I would be grateful for any corrections found in due time. I've divided the kernel into a reusable pure-math layer (Choquet analytic sets, approx minmax etc) and a learning-theory layer that sits on top of it.

[Edit] - This project uses AI in very specific ways. The use was not as simple as "chatgpt write a proof for X". I take active interest in use of AI for writing proofs and have included my observations and methods used in this project in the repo README clearly.
For those inclined, key heuristics used were manually writing core definitions and type structure in one go with sorry placeholders, compiling, then using this checked premise for all AI assisted proof writing, and, asking the AI to list what it knows about it does not know before each step and dividing what uncertainty could be solved using tool use (mathlib greps) and what needed my intervention (handling significant gaps in some classical proof during formalization).

With regards to my project above, can someone specifically guide me on the following? -

  1. Can someone help me figure out if some of the pure math work in the project can constitute a PR?
  2. Is there a plausible fit of some learning theory results in mathlib/adjacent ecosystems like cslib?

I've been working with lean for a while but am new to the community. Excited to connect and learn!
I am working on PAC learning for Algolean using my query framework. It is WIP with a specific target at the moment.
@Samuel Schlesinger already has a cslib PR on the lower bound side for sample complexity.

But this work seems to be heavily AI generated. I don't think any of the major libraries encourage massive AI led PRs. A basic rule of thumb that seems to be emerging is that your first few PRs have to be completely handwritten. It is hard to review such work, and even more difficult to ensure that it can be maintained correctly.

Thanks for the feedback Shreyas and exciting to hear about your work and Samuel's. On "seems heavily AI generated" - I explicitly mention AI use in the About of the repo and in a dedicated methodology section in the project README which details exactly how and where I used frontier models as assistants in this project. I have updated my original post to resolve any remaining confusion on this end. Hope this helps.

Wrt to general consensus on contributing to mathlib - what you said does make sense. It seems I should isolate and handwrite specific portions from the project which might be useful for mathlib/cslib.
